summary:
South Korea does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Legal gender recognition is available and the requirement of surgery is falling. On 8 May 2024 a court ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had been on hormone therapy for years that forcing surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. The Supreme Court has also allowed a transgender person with minor children to change their gender in the family relations register.

Trans visitors have a documented, judicially enforced right to public restrooms. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court issued a final, unappealed ruling that police advice telling a transgender plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, awarding 300,000 won in symbolic compensation against the state.

There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, so services, employment and accommodation carry no statutory protection on these grounds. In healthcare, the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation in November 2023, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients on the grounds that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner. The Constitutional Court did issue a landmark 2024 ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights, extending a measure of recognition in that specific area.

For a visitor on the ground, Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are broadly positive, but the surrounding context requires care: organised conservative opposition is active, no national anti-discrimination law exists, and Human Rights Watch records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people in its 2025 world report, which also notes a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society. No severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented in these sources.

The Seoul Central District Court, presiding judge Chung In-jae, dismissed the state's appeal and ruled partially for the plaintiff in a damages action against the state on 2 July 2024, awarding 300,000 won (about $240) of the 3 million won claimed; the judgment became final because neither party appealed (Korea Times, 22 July 2024). The court held that a police officer's advice to a person mid-legal-transition to avoid public restrooms for a while infringed personal rights, and stated that the right to comfortably use restrooms is a fundamental and universal human right.

The conditions underlying that ruling are quantified by the National Human Rights Commission of Korea's 2021 survey of 591 transgender respondents: 41% had used a restroom of another gender out of fear of mistreatment, 39% restricted food and drink to avoid entering public restrooms, and 36% forwent restroom use altogether. Courts outside the capital have reached the same result against private actors: in 2021 the Pohang branch of the Daegu District Court awarded 7 million won in damages against a beauty academy that barred a transgender student's restroom use.

Recognition has liberalised nationally, not only in the capital. On 8 May 2024 the court in Yeongdong approved male-to-female gender-marker change for five transgender people without sex reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that every human being has the right to live according to their gender identity. The national court guidelines that previously required surgery have been downgraded to reference-only status, though some courts still apply them (Yonhap, 8 May 2024). The ruling sits outside Seoul and bears on this jurisdiction as evidence of the national judicial trend.
tangentialFactors:
Seoul's courts are the clearest rights forum for trans people in South Korea, but the rulings are individual judgments rather than statute: the restroom right rests on personal-rights damages awards, not on an anti-discrimination law, and the surgery requirement for gender-marker change has been loosened by judicial guidance rather than by legislation.

Some courts continue to apply the downgraded national guidelines requiring surgery, so recognition outcomes remain inconsistent between jurisdictions even after the May 2024 decision. A visitor or resident cannot assume that the most liberal recent judgment describes what every court will do.

The national context is mixed. Human Rights Watch's 2025 world report records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people in South Korea while noting a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society, and organised conservative opposition to LGBT rights is active. The absence of a comprehensive anti-discrimination law means the protections that do exist are judicial and reactive.

outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not resolve whether the July 2024 restroom judgment binds private venues, employers or schools; the award ran against the state for police conduct, and the separate 2021 academy judgment shows private actors being liable, but no consolidated rule for private premises is sourced here.

Whether the downgraded reference-only surgical guidelines will continue to produce refusals in some courts, and how often, is not quantified in these materials; the inventory confirms only that some courts still apply them.

Enforcement and incident data are drawn from Seoul and a small number of other courts. Nothing in the inventory establishes equivalent conditions in other South Korean cities, and no source documents a severe incident involving a trans visitor, which reflects an absence of reporting rather than a verified finding of safety.

The precise scope of the 2024 Constitutional Court healthcare ruling for same-sex partners, and any residual effect of the November 2023 refusal to issue hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients on hospital access today, remain unresolved in these sources.
